title: Standard Deviation

findings.finding: Predicting the effect of adding a score equal to the mean requires a relationship that preceding teaching has not explained.
findings.breakdown: Students know how to calculate population standard deviation from complete datasets, but Rachel’s individual scores are unavailable. Adding her mean leaves the mean and extremes unchanged while reducing standard deviation. The qualitative descriptions of spread do not resolve this distinction.
findings.checked: All supplied teaching and practice preceding Q4 were checked. Q1(j–k) provides a useful numerical precursor by removing the mean, but does not identify that feature or explain its effect. Q3(f) changes the frequency of an extreme value. Neither supplies the relationship needed for Q4(c). Q4(d) is adequately supported by the qualitative teaching: zero is far from Rachel’s mean relative to her existing spread, so that target is excluded.
findings.assumptions: The supplied teaching is complete. Students use the calculator methods explicitly taught; no prior rule about adding observations is assumed.

repair.proposal: Before Q4(c), add: 'Compare Q1(j) and (k). Part (k) removes −1.5, the mean of both datasets, and the population standard deviation increases. Reversing this change shows that adding a score equal to the existing mean decreases population standard deviation.'

findings.doneWhen: Students have an explicit connection between the earlier numerical comparison and adding a score at the mean before answering Q4(c).

findings.finding: Compare an equal-dollar pay rise with an equal-percentage pay rise.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up contrasts adding a constant, which preserves standard deviation, with multiplying every value, which scales it.
findings.checked: The original population standard deviation is approximately $191.0444. After multiplying every wage by 1.10, it is approximately $210.1488, giving $210 to the nearest dollar. Calculator calculation is taught, and earlier practice includes proportional changes to datasets.
findings.assumptions: Students use the taught population-standard-deviation calculator method and prior percentage knowledge.

repair.proposal: Append after Q5(b): '(c) Instead of the $20 increase, every employee receives a 10% pay rise. Calculate the new population standard deviation to the nearest dollar.' Expected answer: $210. '(d) Which pay rise gives the smaller standard deviation: $20 each or 10% each?' Expected answer: $20 each.

findings.doneWhen: The two follow-up parts are appended to Q5 with expected answers $210 and $20 each, respectively.
